catalog_quote: Final stressed vowels in content words are always long, and they have been marked with an acute accent. In fact, the accent is not needed on content words consisting of one syllable, but it is useful to distinguish some content words from clitic function words (cf. hí ‘to buy; price’ vs. hi ‘proper article’), and also to indicate where the stress is in two-syllable words with final stress (makí ‘ashamed’). new_statements.quote: The stress on prosodic words is on the penultimate syllable or on the final syllable if the final vowel is long. [...] Final stressed vowels in content words are always long, and they have been marked with an acute accent. [...] The ‘root’ consists of two syllables or one syllable with a long vowel, the first of which is stressed and can contain all vowel sounds (long and short /a/, /i/, /e/, /u/ and /o/ and perhaps some diphthongs). There can be up to two pretonic syllables, of which the vowel is always /a/ [...]. Long vowels are undoubtedly found in all words stressed on the final syllable.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress falls on the penultimate syllable of the prosodic word; it falls on the final syllable only when that syllable has a long vowel (e.g. makí 'ashamed', hí 'buy'), and every finally-stressed vowel is long. Up to two pretonic syllables (vowel always /a/) may precede the stressed root. The authors add that finally-stressed words are historically contractions and a phonemic analysis could posit geminate (bimoraic) final vowels, under which the pattern would reduce to plain penultimate stress; hence provisional reading weight-sensitive (long final vowel attracts stress), with fixed: penultimate syllable as the alternative reading. Unstressed syllables permit only /a i u/; vowel breaking (e>ea, o>oa) occurs in the stressed syllable.
new_statements.exceptions: Words with a long final vowel take final stress (written with acute accent or, in Mitchell 2008a and the Bible translation, with a double vowel). Words with more than one long syllable, more than one post-stress syllable, or pretonic syllables of abnormal shape are treated as compounds (two prosodic words). The authors call the whole grammatical overview preliminary because no grammatical investigation of Wanukaka exists.
new_statements.domain_note: Domain is the prosodic word (dictionary lemma minus clitics), following Klamer's 1998 Kambera model; clitics (e.g. proper article hi) are unstressed. Statement is analytic, not instrumental; the dictionary's 9 IPA transcriptions with a stress mark ( Pronunciation column, from PARADISEC recordings) all show penultimate stress.
new_statements.identity_note: The statement is about Wanukaka proper as spoken in the Wanokaka district (traditional domains Wanokaka and Rua; Glottolog dialects Nuclear Wanukaka and Rua), written by a native-speaker author (Tomas Tagu Dodu, retired university teacher; home village not stated) with two non-speaker redactors. Asplund et al. 2025 say the extent to which Rua differs is unknown and that the Waikabubak variety is heavily influenced by Lolina Weyewa; the statement should be filed at language level wanu1241, not to a dialect code.

sources.note: Nothing Wanukaka-specific on stress. p.141 family-level: 'The epenthetic vowel is extra-metrical and does not shift stress from the penultimate vowel of the root' (Kambera/Weyewa/Mamboru/Kodi examples). pp.141-142: information is conflicting whether Wanukaka has lengthened consonants (Mitchell n.d. 'prolongation of the consonant', 'geminate') or a vowel-length contrast like Laboya; in Lovestrand & Balle's recordings some speakers lengthen, others not.

sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: Nothing for Wanukaka specifically. p.47 fn 27: Wanukaka (Mitchell n.d; author's fieldwork) has the same consonant inventory as Laboya. p.48: stressed-vowel lengthening, 'typically the penultimate syllable', is stated for Weyewa/Kodi, and contrastive vowel length limited to stressed syllables for Kambera/Laboya; Wanukaka not assigned to either type. Notes Mitchell 2008 dictionary and PARADISEC JL4 Wanukaka wordlist (c.300 items).
